newsitem.title: USA: Study says U.S. consumers buy wrong life insurance.
newsitem.headline: Study says U.S. consumers buy wrong life insurance.

text.p: U.S. consumers spend too much on cash life insurance policies that offer little or no return on investment in their early years, according to a study released Wednesday.

The study of 109 whole life and universal life insurance policies, conducted by the non-profit Consumer Federation of America (CFA), found that rates of return vary widely among policies and over time.
"Consumers lose billions of dollars annually by purchasing the wrong policies or not holding onto existing ones," CFA life insurance actuary James Hunt said in a statement.
Broker commissions generally are paid early in the life of a policy, making rates of return negative for the first several years, the federation's report said.
On average, life insurance policies in the study tallied losses of 87.9 percent in year one, 54.9 percent in year two and 18.9 percent in year three. They broke even in year four.
"Only when cash-value policies are held for at least 15 years do (their returns) begin to become at all attractive," the report said.

Consumers should consider purchasing cash-value policies only if they plan to hold them for at least 20 years, but most people already holding such a policy should retain it rather than allowing it to lapse or being talked into a replacement, the federation said.

The federaton recommended two reforms for the cash-value insurance industry: required disclosure of commissions and creation of "suitability laws" to prevent sellers from recommending inappropriate policies.
